title: A1 consolidation
objectives: I can introduce myself in detail: my name, where I am from, where I live, my family and my plans.
I can manage a café, a shop, a meeting with neighbors and small talk with a teacher, and ask someone to repeat or to speak slowly.
I can choose among the five cases met so far for masculine, feminine and neuter nouns and the adjectives that go with them.
I can say 'to have' in two ways, with 'у ме́не є' and with 'ма́ти', and tell the verb 'ма́ти' from the noun 'ма́ти'.
I can join sentences with 'і', 'а', 'але́', 'або́', 'бо', 'тому́' and 'тому́ що', and read this unit's new words with the reading procedure.

vocabulary.note: It adds a person, a thing or an action to what was said before, and it usually stands before the word it adds to or before the verb. It is neutral and fits speech and writing alike.
It means the same as 'тако́ж' but is shorter and more conversational. It is the word in the short reply 'Я теж.', 'Me too.'
It joins two possibilities, mostly in statements. In a question that offers a choice, 'чи' is the usual word: 'Чай чи ка́ва?'

example.target: У субо́ту я чита́ю або́ відпочива́ю.
example.source: On Saturday I read or relax.

vocabulary.note: It introduces a reason and means the same as 'тому́ що', but it is shorter and more conversational. The reason comes after the main statement, with a comma before 'бо'.

example.source: Sam is at home because it is raining.

vocabulary.note: It introduces a result, after the reason has been given. It is the first word of 'тому́ що', 'because': 'тому́ що' points ahead to a reason, and 'тому́' alone points back to one.

example.target: Я з Кана́ди, тому́ говорю́ англі́йською.
example.source: I am from Canada, so I speak English.
example.source_literal: I from Canada, therefore I-speak by-English.

vocabulary.note: Recycled from unit 14, where the note on having first showed 'Він ма́є час.' Regular, like 'чита́ти': 'ма́ю', 'ма́єш', 'ма́ють'. The owner is the subject and the thing owned is the object, in the accusative. It is a different word from the noun 'ма́ти', mother, spelled and stressed the same way.

example.source: I have a brother and a sister.

vocabulary.note: It says that two or more people do something as a group. It usually stands before the verb.

'Жаль' is a masculine noun meaning regret or pity, and 'на' is the preposition 'on'. Inside a sentence the phrase is set off by commas. It also serves as a short reply on its own: 'На жаль, ні.', 'Unfortunately not.'

Its first meaning is 'ordinarily, in the usual way'; from 'as is usual' it came to mean 'of course'. In that sense it is set off by commas or stands alone as a reply. It shares its root with 'зазвича́й', usually.

example.source: Do you want a coffee? Of course!

vocabulary.note: It makes a statement less certain. Used this way it stands outside the rest of the sentence and is set off by commas.

example.source: Perhaps it will be warm tomorrow.

vocabulary.source: excuse me, I beg your pardon
vocabulary.note: It is the 'я' form of the verb 'перепро́шувати', 'to beg pardon', so it says 'I beg pardon'. It is polite with anyone: to apologize, to interrupt or disagree politely, and, as a question, to ask someone to repeat: 'Перепро́шую?', 'Pardon?'

example.source: Excuse me, where is the pharmacy here?

vocabulary.part_of_speech: masculine noun, declined like an adjective
vocabulary.note: It is the adjective 'знайо́мий', familiar or known, used as a noun for a person you know, so it keeps the endings of an adjective: accusative and genitive 'знайо́мого', plural 'знайо́мі'. 'Мій знайо́мий' is the usual way to say 'an acquaintance of mine'.

example.source: An acquaintance of mine works at a bank.

vocabulary.part_of_speech: feminine noun, declined like an adjective
vocabulary.note: The feminine form of the adjective 'знайо́мий' used as a noun, with adjective endings: accusative 'знайо́му', genitive 'знайо́мої'.

example.source: She is an acquaintance of mine.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'сусі́да'; nominative plural 'сусі́ди', which also covers a group of men and women.
Accusative 'сусі́дку', genitive 'сусі́дки'. The 'д' stays voiced before 'к'.
Genitive 'хло́пця': the 'е' drops out, as in 'украї́нець', 'украї́нця'. With a possessive it usually means a boyfriend: 'її́ хло́пець', her boyfriend.

example.target: Хло́пець сиди́ть у па́рку й чита́є.
example.source: A boy is sitting in the park reading.

vocabulary.note: Accusative 'ді́вчину', vocative 'ді́вчино'. With a possessive it usually means a girlfriend: 'його́ ді́вчина', his girlfriend.

dialogues.title: Meeting the neighbors
dialogues.context: On Thursday morning Sam stops by Oksana's building to walk with her to the university. At the entrance they meet her neighbors Liudmyla and Roman, an older couple. The neighbors have known Oksana since she was a child, so they say 'ти' to her; she says 'ви' to them, and Sam and the neighbors say 'ви' to each other. 'Сусі́ди' is the plural of 'сусі́д', and 'знайо́мі' the plural of 'знайо́мий'.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: До́брий ра́нок, па́ні Людми́ло! До́брий ра́нок, па́не Рома́не!
lines.source: Good morning, Ms. Liudmyla! Good morning, Mr. Roman!

lines.speaker: Людми́ла
lines.target: До́брий ра́нок, Окса́но! А хто це? Твій хло́пець?
lines.source: Good morning, Oksana! And who is this? Your boyfriend?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ні, це мій друг Сем. Він з Кана́ди.
lines.source: No, this is my friend Sam. He is from Canada.

lines.speaker: Людми́ла
lines.target: Ду́же приє́мно, Се́ме. Мене́ зва́ти Людми́ла, а це мій чолові́к Рома́н. Ми сусі́ди Окса́ни.
lines.source: Nice to meet you, Sam. My name is Liudmyla, and this is my husband Roman. We are Oksana's neighbors.
lines.source_literal: Very pleasant, Sam. Me to-call Liudmyla, and this my husband Roman. We neighbors of-Oksana.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ду́же приє́мно! Я кана́дець, але́ за́раз живу́ в Ки́єві.
lines.source: Nice to meet you! I am Canadian, but I live in Kyiv now.
lines.source_literal: Very pleasant! I Canadian, but now I-live in Kyiv.

lines.speaker: Рома́н
lines.target: А що ви ро́бите в Ки́єві?
lines.source: And what do you do in Kyiv?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я вивча́ю украї́нську мо́ву. Моя́ вчи́телька, Іри́на Петрі́вна, ду́же до́бра.
lines.source: I am studying Ukrainian. My teacher, Iryna Petrivna, is very good.
lines.source_literal: I study Ukrainian language. My teacher, Iryna Petrivna, very good.

lines.speaker: Людми́ла
lines.target: Ви до́бре гово́рите! А ва́ша сім’я́ теж тут?
lines.source: You speak well! And is your family here too?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ні, на жаль. Мої́ батьки́ живу́ть у Кана́ді.
lines.source: No, unfortunately. My parents live in Canada.
lines.source_literal: No, on regret. My parents live in Canada.

lines.speaker: Рома́н
lines.target: А у вас тут є знайо́мі?
lines.source: And do you know people here?
lines.source_literal: And at you here is acquaintances?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, звича́йно! Окса́на, Тара́с і Оле́на. І ви теж!
lines.source: Yes, of course! Oksana, Taras and Olena. And you too!
lines.source_literal: Yes, ordinarily! Oksana, Taras and Olena. And you too!

lines.speaker: Людми́ла
lines.target: Се́ме, ви ма́єте час у неді́лю? Ми бу́демо роби́ти варе́ники.
lines.source: Sam, do you have time on Sunday? We are going to make varenyky.
lines.source_literal: Sam, you have time on Sunday? We will to-make varenyky.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, ма́ю! Ду́же дя́кую!
lines.source: Yes, I do! Thank you very much!
lines.source_literal: Yes, I-have! Very I-thank!

lines.speaker: Рома́н
lines.target: І ти, Окса́но, звича́йно. Бу́демо обі́дати ра́зом!
lines.source: And you too, Oksana, of course. We will have lunch together!
lines.source_literal: And you, Oksana, ordinarily. We-will to-have-lunch together!

dialogues.title: One Saturday in town
dialogues.context: On Saturday morning, Oksana and Sam go into town. They start at Andrii's café, go on to the secondhand shop where Bohdan works, and then walk out into the street. The friends say 'ти' to each other and 'ви' to Andrii and Bohdan.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: До́брий ра́нок! Що ви хо́чете?
lines.source: Good morning! What would you like?
lines.source_literal: Good morning! What you want?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ка́ву з молоко́м, будь ла́ска. А Сем хо́че чай без цу́кру.
lines.source: A coffee with milk, please. And Sam wants tea without sugar.
lines.source_literal: Coffee with milk, be kindness. And Sam wants tea without sugar.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Окса́но, а що ми ро́бимо по́тім?
lines.source: Oksana, so what are we doing afterward?
lines.source_literal: Oksana, and what we do afterward?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Споча́тку йдемо́ в магази́н, бо я хо́чу нову́ ку́ртку. А по́тім, мо́жливо, у парк або́ на ри́нок.
lines.source: First we're going to a shop, because I want a new jacket. And then perhaps to the park or to the market.
lines.source_literal: First we-go into shop, because I want new jacket. And then, possibly, into park or onto market.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́брий день! Що ви хо́чете приміря́ти?
lines.source: Good afternoon! What would you like to try on?
lines.source_literal: Good day! What you want to-try-on?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Цю жо́вту ку́ртку, будь ла́ска. Се́ме, як ду́маєш?
lines.source: This yellow jacket, please. Sam, what do you think?
lines.source_literal: This yellow jacket, be kindness. Sam, how you-think?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Вона́ ду́же га́рна, але́, мо́жливо, дорога́.
lines.source: It's very nice, but it may be expensive.
lines.source_literal: It very nice, but, possibly, expensive.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Перепро́шую, вона́ не дорога́. Вона́ ко́штує сто гри́вень.
lines.source: Excuse me, but it isn't expensive. It costs a hundred hryvnias.
lines.source_literal: I-beg-pardon, it not expensive. It costs hundred of-hryvnias.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Сто гри́вень? Звича́йно, я її́ купу́ю!
lines.source: A hundred hryvnias? Of course I'm buying it!
lines.source_literal: Hundred of-hryvnias? Ordinarily, I it buy!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Окса́но, іде́ дощ!
lines.source: Oksana, it's raining!
lines.source_literal: Oksana, goes rain!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: На жаль, так. Але́ в ме́не є нова́ ку́ртка!
lines.source: Unfortunately, yes. But I have a new jacket!
lines.source_literal: On regret, yes. But at me is new jacket!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А я сього́дні без ку́ртки. Ти хо́чеш у кафе́?
lines.source: And I don't have a jacket today. Do you want to go to the café?
lines.source_literal: And I today without jacket. You want into café?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, до́бре! Там те́пло, і чай смачни́й.
lines.source: Yes, all right! It's warm there, and the tea is good.
lines.source_literal: Yes, well! There warm, and tea tasty.

dialogues.title: Small talk after class
dialogues.context: On Friday after class, Sam and Iryna Petrivna talk for a few minutes. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other. 'У па́ні Людми́ли' means at Liudmyla's home: 'у' with the genitive of a person, as in 'у ме́не'.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Се́ме, що ви бу́дете роби́ти на вихідни́х?
lines.source: Sam, what will you do on the weekend?
lines.source_literal: Sam, what you will to-do on weekend?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: У субо́ту бу́ду відпочива́ти, а в неді́лю бу́ду обі́дати в па́ні Людми́ли, сусі́дки Окса́ни.
lines.source: On Saturday I'll relax, and on Sunday I'll have lunch at the home of Ms. Liudmyla, Oksana's neighbor.
lines.source_literal: On Saturday I-will to-rest, and on Sunday I-will to-have-lunch at Ms. Liudmyla, neighbor of-Oksana.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Це до́бре. А як спра́ви в Кана́ді? Як ва́ша сім’я́?
lines.source: That's good. And how are things in Canada? How is your family?
lines.source_literal: This good. And how affairs in Canada? How your family?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре, дя́кую. Та́то працю́є в ба́нку, а ма́ма працю́є в шко́лі.
lines.source: Fine, thank you. Dad works at a bank, and Mom works at a school.
lines.source_literal: Well, I-thank. Dad works in bank, and mom works in school.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А брат у вас є?
lines.source: And do you have a brother?
lines.source_literal: And brother at you is?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ні, бра́та в ме́не нема́є. Але́ я ма́ю ді́вчину. Вона́ тако́ж у Кана́ді.
lines.source: No, I don't have a brother. But I have a girlfriend. She is also in Canada.
lines.source_literal: No, of-brother at me there-is-not. But I have girlfriend. She also in Canada.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Вона́ гово́рить украї́нською?
lines.source: Does she speak Ukrainian?
lines.source_literal: She speaks by-Ukrainian?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Тро́хи. Вона́ лю́бить Украї́ну, тому́ теж вивча́є украї́нську мо́ву.
lines.source: A little. She loves Ukraine, so she is learning Ukrainian too.
lines.source_literal: A-little. She loves Ukraine, therefore too studies Ukrainian language.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре! А я в субо́ту ї́ду у Львів. Там живе́ моя́ сестра́.
lines.source: Very good! And on Saturday I'm going to Lviv. My sister lives there.
lines.source_literal: Very well! And I on Saturday go to Lviv. There lives my sister.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: У Львів? А яка́ там пого́да?
lines.source: To Lviv? And what is the weather like there?
lines.source_literal: To Lviv? And what-kind there weather?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: У Льво́ві ча́сто йде дощ, тому́ в ме́не є вели́ка ку́ртка.
lines.source: It often rains in Lviv, so I have a big jacket.
lines.source_literal: In Lviv often goes rain, therefore at me is big jacket.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Перепро́шую, ви мо́жете говори́ти пові́льно?
lines.source: I beg your pardon, could you speak slowly?
lines.source_literal: I-beg-pardon, you can to-speak slowly?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Звича́йно. Там ча́сто йде дощ. Тому́ я ма́ю вели́ку ку́ртку.
lines.source: Of course. It often rains there. So I have a big jacket.
lines.source_literal: Ordinarily. There often goes rain. Therefore I have big jacket.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Розумі́ю! До поба́чення, Іри́но Петрі́вно!
lines.source: I see! Goodbye, Iryna Petrivna!
lines.source_literal: I-understand! Until seeing, Iryna Petrivna!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: перепро́шую, звича́йно, ді́вчина and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
Every new word in this unit can be read with the procedure of the unit on soft sounds, and none needs a new rule. Its seven steps, in short:

- Find the apostrophe: the consonant before it is hard, and the vowel letter after it begins with [j].
- Read each 'я', 'ю' and 'є': [j] plus a vowel at the start of a word, after a vowel or after the apostrophe, and otherwise a plain vowel that softens the consonant before it. 'Ї' is always [ji].
- Look at the letter after each other consonant: a consonant that can be soft is soft before 'і' and 'ь', and hard before 'а', 'о', 'у', 'е', 'и', before another consonant and at the end of a word.
- Join the letters that make one sound: 'дж' and 'дз' within a root, 'щ', and any doubled letter.
- Check each 'в' and the end of the word: 'в' is [ʋ] before a vowel and [w] at the end of a syllable, and voiced consonants stay voiced.
- Find the stress mark and say that syllable louder and longer.
- Say the word slowly, syllable by syllable, then at normal speed.

The unit on stress adds the count of syllables: one for each vowel letter.

'Перепро́шую' [pɛrɛˈprɔʃuju] has five vowel letters, so five syllables, with the stress on the third. Its two unstressed 'е' lean a little toward 'и'. The 'ш' is hard, and the last 'ю' follows a vowel, so it is [j] plus [u]. The word is the 'я' form of 'перепро́шувати', and in the present '-ува-' becomes '-у-', exactly as 'працюва́ти' gives 'працю́ю'.

'Звича́йно' [zʋɪˈt͡ʃɑjnɔ] has three syllables. The 'з' stays voiced before 'в', and the 'в' is [ʋ] because a vowel follows it. The 'ч' is hard, and the 'й' after 'а' closes the syllable, as in 'чай'.

'Ді́вчина' [ˈdʲiwt͡ʃɪnɑ] has three syllables, stressed on the first. The 'д' is soft before 'і'. The 'в' stands before the consonant 'ч', so it is [w], as in 'жо́втий'.

The other new words:

- 'тако́ж' and 'теж' end in 'ж', which stays voiced, as Ukrainian voiced consonants do at the end of a word.
- 'на жаль' is two words of one syllable each, so neither carries a mark; 'жаль' ends in a soft 'л', and the stress of the phrase falls on it.
- 'мо́жливо' keeps its 'ж' voiced before 'л'.
- 'знайо́мий' has 'йо' after a vowel, said [jɔ].
- 'сусі́д' and 'сусі́дка' have a soft 'с' before 'і', and their 'д' stays voiced at the end of a word and before 'к', as in 'шви́дко'.
- 'хло́пець' ends in a soft 'ць', like 'кана́дець', and loses its 'е' in the other forms: 'хло́пця'.
- 'ма́ю', 'ма́єш' and 'ма́ють' have 'ю' and 'є' after a vowel, so each one is [j] plus a vowel.

rows: unstressed 'е' leans to 'и'; 'ю' after a vowel is [ju]

examples.source: I beg your pardon, I don't understand.

examples.target: Ді́вчина й хло́пець сидя́ть у па́рку.
examples.source: A girl and a boy are sitting in the park.

grammar.title: The five cases so far: which job each one does
grammar.explanation:
A case is the form a noun takes to show its job in the sentence. English shows that job with word order and prepositions; Ukrainian shows it with the ending, and a preposition, where there is one, also decides the case of the noun after it. A1 has used five of the seven cases in the singular, and the nominative in the plural as well:

- the nominative, the dictionary form, for the subject
- the vocative, for calling someone
- the accusative, for the direct object and for a direction
- the locative, for a place, always after a preposition
- the genitive, for an owner, for something missing and after many prepositions

To choose the case, find the noun's job first and ask its question: 'хто?' or 'що?' for the subject, 'кого́?' or 'що?' for the object, 'де?' for a place, 'куди́?' for a direction, 'кого́?' or 'чого́?' for an owner. Then look at the preposition. 'У', 'в' and 'на' take the locative when they answer 'де?' and the accusative when they answer 'куди́?'. 'У' or 'в' before a person takes the genitive instead and means 'at the home of' or, with 'є', 'in the possession of': 'у па́ні Людми́ли', 'у ме́не є'. 'Без', 'для', 'до', 'бі́ля' and 'з' meaning 'from' always take the genitive.

A few words bring their own case. 'Нема́є' takes the genitive of what is missing. A day of the week after 'у' or 'в' is in the accusative ('у субо́ту'), and a clock time after 'о' is in the locative ('о сьо́мій'). After a number, 'оди́н' takes the nominative singular and 'два', 'три', 'чоти́ри' the nominative plural; the forms after five and higher, such as 'ро́ків' and 'гри́вень', are still learned whole. A name is in the vocative only when you speak to the person: 'Окса́но, приві́т!', but 'Це Окса́на.'

grammar.title: Masculine nouns and their adjectives in five cases
grammar.explanation:
A masculine noun ends in a consonant, in '-й' or in '-ь' ('брат', 'чай', 'день'). A few end in '-о' ('та́то', 'дя́дько'), and a few in '-а' because they name a man ('Мико́ла'); natural gender wins, so they are masculine in every agreement.

Masculine nouns have two choices that the other genders do not have:

- In the accusative, a person or an animal takes the genitive form ('бра́та', 'кота́'), while a thing keeps the nominative form ('стіл', 'суп').
- In the genitive, people, animals, countable things and most cities take '-а' or '-я' ('бра́та', 'стола́', 'Ки́єва'), while substances, buildings, institutions, places in general and abstract things take '-у' or '-ю' ('су́пу', 'ча́ю', 'па́рку', 'ча́су'). The genitive is learned with each noun.

The locative ends in '-і' ('на столі́', 'у Ки́єві'), written '-ї' after a vowel ('у музе́ї'), and in '-у' for many nouns whose stem ends in 'к', 'г' or 'х' ('у па́рку', 'на ри́нку'). The vocative adds '-е' after a hard consonant ('Тара́се', 'бра́те') and turns '-й' into '-ю' ('Андрі́ю'); 'си́ну' and 'та́ту' are learned as they are.

When an ending is added, the stem can change. An 'і' in the last, closed syllable often goes back to 'о' ('стіл', 'стола́'; 'дім', 'до́му'; 'Львів', 'у Льво́ві'), an 'ї' after a vowel goes back to 'є' ('Ки́їв', 'Ки́єва'), and some nouns lose an 'е' or 'о' ('хло́пець', 'хло́пця'; 'ри́нок', 'на ри́нку').

An adjective or a possessive with a masculine noun ends in '-ий' in the nominative, in '-ого' in the genitive and in the accusative of a person, and in '-ому' in the locative. A soft stem has '-ій', '-ього' and '-ьому': 'си́ній', 'си́нього', 'у си́ньому'. With a thing, the accusative is the nominative form. 'Мій' and 'твій' give 'мого́' and 'твого́'; 'наш' and 'ваш' give 'на́шого' and 'ва́шого'.

rows: нови́й друг, мій чай, цей день
на ново́му столі́, у Ки́єві, у музе́ї
'-а' or '-я': people, animals, countable things, most cities
'-у' or '-ю': substances, places, institutions, abstract things

examples.source: We are sitting in our park.

grammar.title: Feminine nouns and their adjectives in five cases
grammar.explanation:
A feminine noun ends in '-а' or '-я' ('кни́га', 'ку́хня', 'Со́фія') or in a consonant ('сіль', 'о́сінь', 'ніч'). Since many masculine nouns also end in a consonant, the gender of such a noun is learned with it: 'день' is masculine, but 'ніч' is feminine.

A noun in '-а' after a hard consonant has a hard stem ('ма́ма', 'кни́га'). A noun in '-я' has a soft stem, whether the 'я' softens the consonant before it ('ку́хня', 'бабу́ся') or follows a vowel ('Со́фія'). A noun in '-а' after 'ж', 'ч', 'ш' or 'щ' ('пло́ща', 'ї́жа') follows the soft stems in the genitive. The endings:

- Vocative: '-о' for a hard stem ('ма́мо', 'Окса́но'); for names and family words in '-я', '-ю' after a consonant ('бабу́сю', 'О́лю') and '-є' after a vowel ('Со́фіє').
- Accusative: '-у' or '-ю' ('ма́му', 'ку́хню'); a noun in a consonant does not change ('сіль').
- Locative: '-і', written '-ї' after a vowel ('у Со́фії'), before which 'г', 'к', 'х' become 'з', 'ц', 'с' ('у кни́зі', 'в апте́ці', 'у руці́').
- Genitive: '-и' after a hard stem ('ма́ми', 'сестри́'), '-і' after a soft stem, after 'ж', 'ч', 'ш', 'щ' and for a noun in a consonant ('бабу́сі', 'пло́щі', 'со́лі'), written '-ї' after a vowel ('Со́фії').

Stress can move between the forms: 'сестра́' has the genitive 'сестри́' but the nominative plural 'се́стри', and 'рука́' has the accusative 'ру́ку'. Learn the stress with each form you meet.

An adjective with a feminine noun ends in '-а' in the nominative, '-у' in the accusative, '-ій' in the locative and '-ої' in the genitive; a soft stem has '-я', '-ю', '-ій' and '-ьої' ('си́ня', 'си́ню', 'у си́ній', 'си́ньої'). The possessives follow: 'моя́', 'мою́', 'у мої́й', 'моє́ї'; 'на́ша', 'на́шу', 'у на́шій', 'на́шої'. 'Па́ні' never changes.

rows: '-о' for a hard stem; '-ю' or '-є' for names in '-я'
у нові́й кни́зі, на мої́й ку́хні, в апте́ці
'-і' after a soft stem, after 'ж', 'ч', 'ш', 'щ', and for a consonant noun

examples.source: We will have lunch in the kitchen.

grammar.title: Neuter nouns and their adjectives in five cases
grammar.explanation:
A neuter noun ends in '-о' ('вікно́', 'мі́сто'), in '-е' ('со́нце') or in '-я' after a doubled consonant ('життя́'). A few other nouns in '-я' are neuter too, such as 'перехре́стя' and 'ім’я́', but most nouns in '-я' are feminine ('ку́хня', 'пі́сня'), so the gender of a noun in '-я' is learned with it. Loanwords that never change, such as 'кафе́', 'меню́' and 'метро́', are neuter too, and they keep one form in every case: 'у кафе́', 'без меню́'.

Neuter nouns are the simplest of the three genders:

- The accusative is always the same as the nominative: 'Я ба́чу вікно́.'
- The vocative is also the same as the nominative; neuter nouns rarely name someone you speak to.
- The locative ends in '-і', before which 'к' becomes 'ц': 'у мі́сті', 'на о́зері', 'у молоці́', 'у я́блуці'. Nouns in '-я' take '-і' as well: 'у житті́', 'на перехре́сті'.
- The genitive ends in '-а', or '-я' for the nouns in '-я': 'мі́ста', 'вікна́', 'молока́', 'життя́'.

The stress often moves between the genitive singular and the nominative plural, and in some nouns it is the only difference between them: 'мі́ста' is 'of the city', but 'міста́' is 'cities'; 'вікна́' is 'of the window', but 'ві́кна' is 'windows'.

An adjective or a possessive with a neuter noun has every form of the masculine except the nominative and the accusative, which end in '-е', or '-є' for a soft stem: 'нове́ вікно́', 'си́нє вікно́', 'моє́ мі́сто', 'на́ше мі́сто'. The locative is 'у ново́му мі́сті', and the genitive 'ново́го мі́ста', 'мого́ мі́ста'.

rows: нове́ вікно́, вели́ке мі́сто, моє́ життя́
у вели́кому мі́сті, на о́зері, у молоці́

examples.source: We live in a big city.
This is the center of the city.

grammar.title: Verbs so far: the present, reflexive verbs and the future with 'бу́ду'
grammar.explanation:
A Ukrainian verb in the present has its own ending for each person, so the pronoun can be left out: 'чита́ю' alone means 'I read'. There are two conjugations, two sets of endings:

- first conjugation: '-у' or '-ю', '-еш' or '-єш', '-е' or '-є', '-емо' or '-ємо', '-ете' or '-єте', '-уть' or '-ють' ('чита́ти', 'працюва́ти', 'жи́ти', 'писа́ти', 'ма́ти')
- second conjugation: '-у' or '-ю', '-иш' or '-їш', '-ить' or '-їть', '-имо' or '-їмо', '-ите' or '-їте', '-ать' or '-ять' ('говори́ти', 'роби́ти', 'люби́ти', 'сиді́ти', 'стоя́ти', 'спа́ти')

Most verbs in '-ити' belong to the second conjugation, and most in '-ати', '-яти' and '-ува́ти' to the first. Some stems change in the present, and the 'я' and 'ти' forms show the change and the stress: 'працю́ю' ('-ува-' becomes '-у-'), 'живу́', 'пишу́', 'роблю́' and 'люблю́' (an 'л' after 'б'), 'сиджу́'. A few verbs are irregular and are learned whole: 'хо́чу', 'їм', 'п’ю', 'іду́', 'ї́ду', 'мо́жу'.

A reflexive verb carries the suffix '-ся' after the personal ending: 'одяга́юся', 'одяга́єшся', 'одяга́ється'. After a vowel '-ся' can be shortened to '-сь' ('одяга́юсь'). In '-ться' and '-шся' the sound differs from the spelling: 'одяга́ється' ends in [t͡sʲːɑ], and 'одяга́єшся' in [sʲːɑ].

The future of an imperfective verb is the future of 'бу́ти' plus the infinitive: 'бу́ду', 'бу́деш', 'бу́де', 'бу́демо', 'бу́дете', 'бу́дуть' ('Я бу́ду відпочива́ти.'). 'Бу́де' alone means 'will be' ('За́втра бу́де те́пло.'). A plan that is already fixed can also be told in the present, usually with a word of time, as English does with 'I am going to Lviv on Saturday': 'У субо́ту я ї́ду у Львів.'

examples.source: Do you often have breakfast at home?

examples.target: У неді́лю ми бу́демо обі́дати ра́зом.
examples.source: On Sunday we will have lunch together.
examples.source_literal: On Sunday we will to-have-lunch together.

grammar.title: Two ways to say 'to have': 'у ме́не є' and 'ма́ти'
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian has two ways to say that someone has something, and both are standard.

The first, from the unit on the family, makes the thing owned the subject: 'У ме́не є брат.', literally 'at me is brother'. The owner stands after 'у' in the genitive ('у ме́не', 'у те́бе', 'в Окса́ни'), and 'є' says that the thing exists. In the negative, 'нема́є' takes the place of 'є', and the thing missing is in the genitive: 'У ме́не нема́є бра́та.'

The second uses the verb 'ма́ти', to have, which is built like English 'have': the owner is the subject, and the thing owned is the direct object, in the accusative. 'Ма́ти' is a regular verb of the first conjugation, like 'чита́ти': 'ма́ю', 'ма́єш', 'ма́є', 'ма́ємо', 'ма́єте', 'ма́ють'. Because the object is in the accusative, a feminine noun in '-а' or '-я' changes and a masculine person takes '-а': 'Я ма́ю сестру́.', 'Я ма́ю бра́та.' After 'не ма́ти' the thing missing is usually in the genitive, as after 'нема́є': 'Я не ма́ю ча́су.'

For owning things and having relatives, both are correct. 'У ме́не є' is the most frequent way to say what you own and which relatives you have. 'Ма́ти' is just as natural, and it is the usual verb in the expression 'ма́ти час', to have time: 'Ти ма́єш час у субо́ту?'

The verb 'ма́ти', to have, and the noun 'ма́ти', mother, are two different words with the same spelling and the same stress. The noun is feminine and has the genitive 'ма́тері'; the verb has personal endings ('ма́ю', 'ма́є') and takes an object. In 'Моя́ ма́ти ма́є сестру́.', 'My mother has a sister', the word 'ма́ти' is the noun, and 'ма́є' is the form of the verb for 'вона́'.

grammar.title: Joining sentences: 'і', 'а', 'але́', 'або́', 'бо', 'тому́' and 'тому́ що'
grammar.explanation:
Most words that join words or sentences are conjunctions: words whose only job is to join, and which stand between the two parts they join. 'Тому́', 'тако́ж' and 'теж' are adverbs instead. Each belongs to one of the two sentences and adds a meaning to it, so it can stand after another word of that sentence: 'Я теж удо́ма.'

- 'і' and 'й' are one conjunction, 'and', in two forms chosen by euphony: 'й' after a vowel before a consonant, 'і' elsewhere ('Окса́на й Тара́с', 'Тара́с і Окса́на').
- 'а' is 'and' with a contrast or a change of subject: 'Я тут, а ти там.'
- 'але́' is 'but', for what goes against what you would expect: 'Ку́ртка га́рна, але́ дорога́.'
- 'або́' is 'or' between two possibilities, mostly in statements; in a question that offers a choice, 'or' is usually 'чи': 'Чай чи ка́ва?'
- 'бо' and 'тому́ що' both mean 'because' and introduce the reason, after the main statement. 'Бо' is shorter and more conversational.
- 'тому́' means 'so' or 'therefore' and introduces the result, after the reason. It is the first word of 'тому́ що': 'тому́ що' points ahead to a reason, while 'тому́' alone points back to one already given.
- 'тако́ж' and 'теж' mean 'also' or 'too'; 'теж' is more conversational.

A comma goes before 'а', 'але́', 'бо', 'тому́ що' and 'тому́' when they join two sentences. No comma goes before 'і' or 'або́' when they join two words.

rows: Я вдо́ма, тому́ що йде дощ.

examples.target: Окса́на й Сем ї́дуть у центр.
examples.source: Oksana and Sam are going downtown.

examples.target: Сем лю́бить ка́ву, а Тара́с лю́бить чай.
examples.source: Sam likes coffee, and Taras likes tea.

examples.target: Я хо́чу в парк, але́ йде дощ.
examples.source: I want to go to the park, but it is raining.
examples.source_literal: I want into park, but goes rain.

examples.target: У неді́лю ми обі́даємо вдо́ма або́ в кафе́.
examples.source: On Sunday we have lunch at home or at a café.

examples.source: I don't have time, so I don't have breakfast.
examples.source_literal: I not have of-time, therefore not I-have-breakfast.

grammar.title: Four choices to check: 'и' or 'і', 'де' or 'куди́', 'у' or 'на', and agreement
grammar.explanation:
Four choices account for most beginners' mistakes, and each one has a rule you can check.

'И' and 'і' are two different vowels: 'и' is [ɪ] as in 'sit', 'і' is [i] as in 'see'. The letter can change the word ('кит', whale, against 'кіт', cat), and 'і' softens 'д', 'т', 'з', 'с', 'ц', 'л' and 'н' before it, while 'и' never does: 'ді́вчина' has a soft 'д', 'дити́на' a hard one. In endings the two letters carry grammar: 'нови́й стіл', a new table, against 'нові́ столи́', new tables.

'Де?' asks where someone or something is, and the answer has the locative: 'Де ти? Я в па́рку.' 'Куди́?' asks where to, and the answer has the accusative: 'Куди́ ти йдеш? Я йду в парк.' Verbs of going, such as 'іти́' and 'ї́хати', go with 'куди́?'; verbs of being somewhere, such as 'жи́ти', 'працюва́ти' and 'сиді́ти', go with 'де?'.

'У' or 'в' is for the inside of something and for cities and countries ('у шко́лі', 'у Ки́єві', 'в Украї́ні'). 'На' is for surfaces, open places, events and some institutions, and it is learned with each noun ('на столі́', 'на пло́щі', 'на по́шті', 'на робо́ті', 'на ку́хні'). A noun keeps its preposition for the direction: 'на по́шті', 'на по́шту'; 'у па́рку', 'у парк'.

An adjective, a possessive or a demonstrative copies the gender, number and case of its noun, and the gender belongs to the noun. Learn each noun with 'мій', 'моя́' or 'моє́': 'мій день', but 'моя́ ніч'; 'мій та́то', because natural gender wins over the ending; 'моє́ життя́'.

де? asks for a place: locative
куди́? asks for a direction: accusative
у шко́лі, у Ки́єві, в Украї́ні
на: surfaces, open places, events, some institutions
на столі́, на пло́щі, на по́шті

мій день, моя́ ніч, моє́ життя́

Where are you going? To Lviv.

culture.title: Neighbors, guests and small talk
culture.text:
Many people in Ukrainian cities live in large apartment buildings, and neighbors meet every day at the entrance and on the stairs. They greet each other with 'До́брий день' or 'До́брий ра́нок', even when they do not know each other well. Older neighbors who have known a young person since childhood say 'ти' to them, and the young person answers with 'ви' and, to be polite, with 'па́ні' or 'па́не' and the vocative of the first name, as Oksana does with 'па́ні Людми́ло'.

'Як спра́ви?' is a real question among people who know each other, and the answer can be a few sentences about family or work as well as a short 'До́бре, дя́кую'. Among strangers small talk is brief: someone serving you in a shop greets you but does not usually ask how you are.

An invitation to lunch at home on a Sunday is a sign of friendship. A guest usually follows a few customs:

- bring something small, such as a cake, sweets or flowers
- give flowers in an odd number, because even numbers are for funerals
- take off your shoes at the door, where the hosts often offer slippers
- expect a lot of food, and expect to be offered more

Before the meal people wish each other 'Смачно́го!', and afterward the guest thanks the hosts with 'Дя́кую!'. Varenyky made together at home, as Liudmyla and Roman plan, are a typical meal for a family Sunday.

exercises.prompt: Match each word or phrase with its English meaning
Match each joining word with its job

exercises.explanation: 'Кіт' has 'і' [i], as in 'see'. 'Кит' has 'и' [ɪ], as in 'sit', and means 'whale'; 'ніс' is 'nose'.

exercises.audio_target: На жаль, сього́дні я не працю́ю.
choices: Of course, I am working today.
Unfortunately, I am not working today.
Unfortunately, I am not working tomorrow.
[w], as in 'cow', because the consonant 'ч' follows it
exercises.explanation: Before a consonant 'в' is [w], as in 'жо́втий': [ˈdʲiwt͡ʃɪnɑ]. It is [ʋ] only before a vowel, and it never becomes [f].

choices: It is the 'я' form of 'перепро́шувати', and in the present '-ува-' becomes '-у-', as in 'працю́ю'
It belongs to the second conjugation
exercises.explanation: Verbs in '-ува́ти' drop '-ва-' in the present and keep the 'у': 'перепро́шувати', 'перепро́шую', just as 'працюва́ти', 'працю́ю'. The final 'ю' follows a vowel, so it is [ju].

exercises.prompt: In the genitive 'хло́пця', what has happened to the 'е' of 'хло́пець'?
choices: It has dropped out, as in 'украї́нець', 'украї́нця'
exercises.explanation: Some masculine nouns lose an 'е' or 'о' of the last syllable when an ending is added: 'хло́пець', 'хло́пця'; 'украї́нець', 'украї́нця'; 'ри́нок', 'на ри́нку'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'знайо́мий', acquaintance, have the endings of an adjective?
choices: It is an adjective meaning 'familiar' used as a noun for a person you know
All masculine nouns for people end in '-ий'
It is a masculine noun in the plural
exercises.explanation: 'Знайо́мий' began as the adjective 'familiar, known'. Used as a noun for a person, it kept its adjective endings: 'знайо́мого', plural 'знайо́мі'.
'Ма́ти' is conjugated like 'чита́ти', so the 'я' form is 'ма́ю'. The sister is the object, in the accusative: 'сестру́'.
In 'у ме́не є' the brother is the subject, in the nominative, and 'є' says that he exists.

exercises.hint_source: Taras is at home, and I am at home too.
exercises.explanation: 'Теж' and 'тако́ж' both mean 'also' or 'too', and 'теж' is more conversational. Either one stands before the word it adds to.

exercises.hint_source: I'm at home because it's raining.
exercises.explanation: The reason follows, so the word is 'бо' or 'тому́ що', which both mean 'because'. 'Бо' is more conversational.

exercises.hint_source: Sam is from Canada, so he speaks English.
exercises.explanation: The result follows the reason, so the word is 'тому́', 'so, therefore'.

exercises.hint_source: I'm going to the post office.
exercises.explanation: 'По́шта' takes 'на': 'на по́шті' for the place and 'на по́шту', with the accusative, for the direction.
A city takes 'у' or 'в', and before 'льв' the form is always 'у'. 'Льво́ві' is the locative, the case of place.
'Сестри́' is the feminine genitive of the owner, so 'моя́' takes the genitive ending too: 'моє́ї'.
A friend is a person, so the masculine accusative has the genitive form: 'дру́га', and 'мій' becomes 'мого́'.
'Прокида́тися' is a reflexive verb: the 'вона́' form 'прокида́є' takes the suffix '-ся'. After the consonant of '-ть' only '-ся' is possible, and '-ться' is said [t͡sʲːɑ].
After 'не ма́ти' the thing missing is usually in the genitive. 'Час' is abstract, so its genitive ends in '-у': 'ча́су'.

exercises.hint_source: We are sitting in a big park.
exercises.explanation: 'Па́рку' is a masculine locative, so the adjective takes '-ому': 'у вели́кому па́рку'.

exercises.prompt: Which question asks where someone is going?
exercises.explanation: 'Куди́?' asks for a direction, answered with the accusative ('У парк.'). 'Де?' asks where someone is, answered with the locative.
'Ніч' ends in a consonant but is feminine, so 'my' is 'моя́'. The gender of a noun in a consonant is learned with the noun.
The genitive singular 'мі́ста' keeps the stress of 'мі́сто'. 'Міста́', stressed on the ending, is the nominative plural, 'cities', and 'мі́сті' is the locative, as in 'у мі́сті'.

exercises.prompt: In 'Моя́ ма́ти ма́є бра́та.', which word is a form of the verb 'to have'?
exercises.explanation: 'Ма́є' is the 'вона́' form of the verb 'ма́ти'. The word 'ма́ти' here is the noun 'mother', the subject, and 'бра́та' is the object in the accusative.

exercises.prompt: In 'Я ма́ю ді́вчину.', why does 'ді́вчина' end in '-у'?
choices: It follows 'нема́є', so it is in the genitive
It is the object of 'ма́ю', so it is in the accusative
It is the subject, so it is in the nominative
exercises.explanation: With 'ма́ти' the thing or person you have is the object, in the accusative. With 'у ме́не є' it would be the subject: 'У ме́не є ді́вчина.'

exercises.prompt: At the entrance of her building, why does Liudmyla say 'ти' to Oksana but 'ви' to Sam?
choices: She has known Oksana since childhood, and she has only just met Sam
exercises.explanation: Older neighbors say 'ти' to a young person they have known since childhood. Sam is an adult she has just met, so she says 'ви'.

exercises.prompt: In the shop, Bohdan says 'Перепро́шую, вона́ не дорога́.' What does 'перепро́шую' do here?
exercises.explanation: 'Перепро́шую', 'I beg pardon', softens what follows: Bohdan politely disagrees with Sam about the price.

exercises.prompt: Iryna Petrivna first says 'в ме́не є вели́ка ку́ртка' and then 'я ма́ю вели́ку ку́ртку'. Why does the jacket change its ending?
choices: In the first sentence it is the subject, in the nominative; in the second it is the object of 'ма́ю', in the accusative
The second sentence is in the future
The second sentence is about two jackets
exercises.explanation: Both sentences mean 'I have a big jacket'. With 'у ме́не є' the jacket is the subject; with 'ма́ти' it is the object, so the feminine '-а' becomes '-у'.

exercises.audio_target: Це мій сусі́д і його́ ді́вчина.
exercises.hint_source: This is my neighbor and his girlfriend.

exercises.prompt_source: Do you have time on Saturday?
I have a brother and a sister.

exercises.explanation: Both ways are standard: with 'у' and the genitive 'Оле́ни' the brother is the subject, 'брат'; with 'ма́ти' he is the object, 'бра́та'. At the start of a sentence before a vowel, euphony gives 'в'.
There is no word for 'is', and 'моя́' agrees with the feminine 'сусі́дка'.

exercises.prompt_source: Where are you going? (on foot, to a friend)
exercises.explanation: A direction takes 'куди́', walking is 'іти́', and after the vowel of 'ти' euphony gives 'йдеш'.

exercises.prompt_source: It's raining, so we are at home.
exercises.explanation: 'Іде́ дощ' is literally 'goes rain', and 'тому́' introduces the result. After the vowel of 'ми', 'вдо́ма' keeps its 'в'.
